mumun-pottery-period.name: Mumun period
mumun-pottery-period.summary: A Korean prehistoric era, roughly 1500 to 300 BC, named for plain pottery and marked by the rise of intensive agriculture and complex societies on the Korean Peninsula and in Japan.

jeulmun-pottery-period.name: Jeulmun pottery period
jeulmun-pottery-period.summary: An archaeological era in Korean prehistory lasting from about 8000 to 1500 BCE, named for its distinctive comb-patterned pottery, covering Korea's Mesolithic and Neolithic stages.

dolmen.name: Dolmen
dolmen.summary: A type of single-chamber megalithic tomb of upright stones topped with a large flat capstone, mostly built in the Late Neolithic period, 4000 to 3000 BCE.

dog.name: Dogū
dog.summary: Small humanoid and animal clay figurines made in Japan's later Jōmon period (14,000–400 BCE); their purpose remains unknown.

hollow-dog.name: Hollow Dogū
hollow-dog.summary: A Japanese clay figurine from the Late Jōmon period, about 1500 to 1300 BC, found in Hokkaido and one of only five dogū designated a National Treasure.

j-mon-period.name: Jōmon period
j-mon-period.summary: Era in Japanese history from about 14,000 to 300 BC when Japan was inhabited by the Jōmon culture, known for bone, stone and shell tools and jewelry, pottery and lacquerware.

national-treasure-japan.name: National Treasure
national-treasure-japan.summary: Japan's highest legal designation for buildings, artwork and crafts of exceptional cultural or historical value, chosen by the Agency for Cultural Affairs from a wider list of Important Cultural Properties.

old-chos-n.name: Gojoseon
old-chos-n.summary: The first kingdom on the Korean Peninsula, traditionally said to have been founded by the legendary Tan'gun in 2333 BCE, ending in 108 BCE when Han China defeated it.

tan-gun.name: Tan'gun
tan-gun.summary: Legendary founder and first king of Gojoseon, Korea's first kingdom, said in the 13th-century Samguk yusa to have founded it in 2333 BC as the grandson of heaven and son of a bear.

hwanung.name: Hwanung
hwanung.summary: In Korean mythology, the son of the heavenly Lord Hwanin who, with his ministers of clouds, rain and wind, instituted laws and taught humans arts, medicine and agriculture.

ungnyeo.name: Ungnyeo
ungnyeo.summary: Bear who became a woman in the Korean creation myth, wife of the divine king Hwanung and mother of Dangun, the legendary founder of Korea.

samguk-yusa.name: Samguk yusa
samguk-yusa.summary: A collection of Korean legends and historical accounts compiled by the Buddhist monk Il-yeon around 1280; it holds the earliest surviving record of the Dangun founding legend.

book-of-wei.name: Book of Wei
book-of-wei.summary: A Chinese historical text compiled by Wei Shou between 551 and 554, covering the Northern Wei and Eastern Wei dynasties from 386 to 550.

taebaeksan.name: Taebaeksan
taebaeksan.summary: A South Korean mountain in the Taebaek range, part of the Baekdu-daegan system, designated the country's 22nd national park in 2016.

emperor-yao.name: Emperor Yao
emperor-yao.summary: Legendary Chinese ruler traditionally dated to around 2356–2255 BCE, regarded by some sources as one of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.

veritable-records-of-the-joseon-dynasty.name: Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty
veritable-records-of-the-joseon-dynasty.summary: State-compiled annals documenting the reigns of Korea's Joseon dynasty kings from 1392 to 1865, comprising 1,893 volumes and considered the longest continuous record of a single dynasty.
veritable-records-of-the-joseon-dynasty.source_title: Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty

tongguk-t-onggam.name: Tongguk t'onggam
tongguk-t-onggam.summary: A 15th-century Korean chronicle compiled under kings Sejo and Seongjong, the earliest surviving record to list the rulers of Gojoseon after Dangun.

tengri.name: Tengri
tengri.summary: The sky god of traditional Turkic and Mongolic beliefs, seen as eternal, supreme, and the judge and source of life; worship centered on him is called Tengrism.

guanzi-text.name: Guanzi
guanzi-text.summary: An anonymous ancient Chinese political and philosophical text compiled in the early Han dynasty, covering ideas such as price regulation of commodities.

il-yeon.name: Il-yeon
il-yeon.summary: A Korean Buddhist monk (1206–1289) of the Goryeo dynasty who became a monk at nine, was later honored as National Preceptor, and wrote the surviving Samguk Yusa.

sima-guang.name: Sima Guang
sima-guang.summary: Chinese historian and Song dynasty official, 1019–1086, who wrote the monumental Zizhi Tongjian and opposed Wang Anshi's reform policies.

zizhi-tongjian.name: Zizhi Tongjian
zizhi-tongjian.summary: A Chinese historical chronicle presented in 1084, covering 403 BC to 959 AD across 16 dynasties, compiled over 19 years by official Sima Guang (1019-1086).

chewang-un-gi.name: Chewang un'gi
chewang-un-gi.summary: A 1287 Korean historical poem by Yi Sŭnghyu tracing history from Dangun to King Chungnyeol, notable as the first text to treat Balhae as part of Korean history.

kija-chos-n.name: Jizi (Kija)
kija-chos-n.summary: Legendary Shang dynasty sage said to have founded the Kija Chosŏn dynasty of ancient Korea, said to have reigned from 1120 to 194 BCE.

shang-dynasty.name: Shang dynasty
shang-dynasty.summary: A Chinese royal dynasty that ruled the Yellow River valley in the 2nd millennium BCE, the earliest Chinese dynasty confirmed by archaeology, known for oracle-bone writing found at its capital near Anyang.

baiyue.name: Baiyue
baiyue.summary: Various ethnic groups living across southern China and northern Vietnam during the 1st millennia BC and AD, known for short hair, tattoos and skilled seafaring, later assimilated into Chinese culture.

j-mon-pottery.name: Jōmon pottery
j-mon-pottery.summary: Ancient earthenware made in Japan's Jōmon period, among the earliest pottery known, decorated with rope-pressed cord patterns; later forms include elaborate flame and crown-shaped vessels.
